fields.introduction: Investigate colonial tribute, payment forms, household burdens, collection records and changing tax systems.

fields.lessonRecap: A colonial obligation was recorded, not necessarily a voluntary gift. Recorded payment does not prove that a person approved of the demand. Goods could be involved in that setting; other collections need their own evidence. A named item does not establish one amount or form for every community. The same demand can leave different resources available. Equal amounts demanded do not automatically mean equal burdens. Compare their dates, coverage and recorded actions before explaining the difference. A complaint needs follow-up evidence to establish its outcome. One system ended while a later personal-tax system followed. A dated payment needs the rule that applied in its own setting.

fields.title: A Required Payment, Not a Gift
fields.content:
Tribute was a required payment under Spanish colonial authority. It was not simply a freely chosen present. Collecting it brought resources into the colonial system. To understand a demand, ask who required payment, who was expected to pay, and what rule applied in that place and period. A label such as tax does not tell us whether a collection was fair.

Imagine two fictional cards. One describes a family choosing a gift; the other records a payment demanded by an authority. The second describes an obligation: something people were required to do. Do not call it voluntary just because a record says it was paid. A payment record also does not show that every resident agreed with the demand. We study this system to understand people and power, not to reward collecting from classmates.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.

fields.title: Payments Could Involve Goods
fields.content:
Payments did not always consist only of coins. Early colonial accounts describe goods such as rice, cotton, cloth and wax being collected as tribute in particular places. The kind of payment depended on the rule and setting. An example of cloth tribute does not mean that every household everywhere paid the same cloth or amount.

A study in The Philippine Review of Economics discusses woven goods in early tribute and trade. This helps keep the work of makers visible: cloth had to be produced before it could be collected. Our pictured bundle is a modern teaching symbol, not an original tribute item or a measurement guide. When you read a record, look for its place, date, item and unit. Do not change an example into a universal payment schedule.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.

fields.title: What Did a Payment Mean for a Household?
fields.content:
A required payment could affect what a household had available for its other needs. Goods required materials and work. Money required access to money. To explain the burden, we need more than the size of a demand: we also need to know what resources people had and what conditions they faced. This mission does not assign one experience to every family.

Try a fictional comparison, not a historical tax rate. Household A has ten supply tokens and Household B has five. Both must give two. A has eight left and B has three. The same number taken leaves different amounts available. The tokens stand for resources only; they are not pesos, real tribute rates or points earned for taking goods. To explain an actual case, find evidence about the demand and the household circumstances.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.

fields.title: Read the Rule and the Collection Separately
fields.content:
A rule can describe what an authority demanded. A collection record can describe what was received. These are related questions, but they are not the same. A rule alone does not prove that every demanded payment was collected. A recorded collection alone does not settle whether it followed the rule or how it affected the people who paid.

Our fictional source desk has three cards: a payment instruction, a collection entry, and a complaint about an extra demand. The instruction helps identify the rule. The entry helps identify a recorded action. The complaint helps identify a reported problem; it does not by itself show how the problem was finally resolved. Compare the cards rather than treating any one as a complete account. Colonial writers had their own purposes, and their records may leave local voices out.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.

fields.title: Tax Rules Changed Over Time
fields.content:
Spanish colonial rule lasted for a long period, and taxation did not stay unchanged throughout it. Historian Filomeno Aguilars study identifies the ending of tribute in 1884 and the introduction of cedulas personales in 1885. A cedula personal was connected with a later personal-tax system. Keep these two stages distinct instead of treating every colonial payment as the same rule.

The study explains that the later system used rates connected with economic capacity. That does not mean taxation ended, that every person paid the same amount, or that everyone welcomed the change. Our timeline marks the transition described in this study; it is not a complete chart of every tax. A real payment record still needs its own date, category and setting. We are comparing historical systems, not giving instructions about modern taxes.

Open the three clues. Then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help, and return to the lesson before practice when a topic needs review.

fields.title: Prepare Your Tribute Investigation Report
fields.content:
Review five ideas from this mission. Tribute was a required colonial payment rather than simply a gift. Payments could include goods in particular settings. The burden depended on available resources as well as the demand. Rules and recorded collections answer different questions. Tax systems also changed over time.

Prepare a fictional museum report for another Grade 5 learner. State what was demanded, identify the supporting source and explain what you cannot yet know. If you use the two-token household model, label it as a model. It is not a historical tribute rate. Do not assume all households had the same experience or that payment proves agreement.

Your main quiz has five questions. Three correct passes this mission. If you need help, the review path leads back to learning content before targeted practice and a retry. Only Chapter 9 Mission 1 is ready in this release. Completing it does not complete the chapter or award its final badge; Missions 2-5 and the challenge are still being prepared.
